name: Pumpkin
lede: Pumpkin is the saturated orange of the squash, a name that works as a plain, learnable shade of orange and carries two small stories: Cinderella's coach and a Dutch king's cloak.

sections.title: The orange of a squash
sections.body: Paterson glosses *pumpkin* as the orange-yellow of the pumpkin [1]. Pastoureau lists it with *apricot*, *saffron* and *tan* as alternatives for the word *orange*, and warns that swapping them in would change the connotations of the color [2]. Pastoureau notes the words have no true synonyms, so each opens a wider field of connotation [2]. Pumpkin sits beside [[apricot]] and [[tangerine]] as a way to name a shade of [[orange]].

sections.title: Cinderella's coach
sections.body: Pastoureau notes that in Perrault's version of Cinderella a pumpkin becomes a carriage, rats become coachmen and lizards become valets [3]. Finlay describes a squat carriage in Cremona, made in 1663, as the kind of little pumpkin Cinderella could have fled the ball in, and says it is the same reddish orange [4].

sections.title: A cloak for the House of Orange
sections.body: St Clair describes a portrait of William III, attributed to Thomas Murray, in which he wears a voluminous flame-colored velvet cloak trimmed with ermine, with two large silk tassels, in an eye-catching shade of pumpkin [5]. She adds that the Dutch embraced the color enthusiastically out of gratitude to William I, and that the exact shade they favored has shifted over the years [5].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is #FF7518, the web's "pumpkin" orange, fully saturated and fairly bright [6]. Dictionary values are screen approximations, and a real pumpkin ranges from yellow-orange to a dull brownish orange [1][6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The match is almost absent from the painted record: only 1 of 23,781 canvases in the ColorHub archive holds this color across at least 5% of the picture, a Pahari painting from India dated 1810, as photographed [6].

notes.cite: St Clair, The Secret Lives of Colour, ch. 46 ("Orange")

questions.q: In Perrault's Cinderella, what does the pumpkin become?
St Clair says the Dutch took to which shade after William I?

openers: In Perrault's Cinderella, a pumpkin becomes a carriage [3].

issues: Cloak was William III (portrait attributed to Murray), not William I; Dutch gratitude was to William I
Pastoureau's word list is about the French orangé; reworded
